searchText: I just published the idea for "ReGenesis": https://ethresear.ch/t/regenesis-resetting-ethereum-to-reduce-the-burden-of-large-blockchain-and-state/7582 Hmm, not sure I understand this idea Is it basically saying that we agree on a one-time event where all state and history before some time X is no longer considered available, and so accessing anything from there requires a witness? yes. And it does not have to be one-time. We can do it regularly That feels like it already incurs most of the complexity of stateless ethereum yes, but it does not requite repricing for the sake of witnesses Actually isn't it basically the same as the "half-stateless ethereum where witnesses don't include anything accessed in the last N blocks" but discrete instead of continuous? it is very similar, yes eh IMO we have to do the repricing anyway because the things that are bad for witness size are also bad for DoS attacks at present The DoS vulnerability would be lower with a smaller state size but only logarithmically so I don't think there will be vulnerability, because attacker will have to pay for the proofs no I mean DoS transactions that access a bunch of contracts that are already in the "fresh state" So same sort of thing that an attacker would do today oh, to expand the fresh state? No, to hit disk over and over again As fresh state would still go on disk same as today, right? well, if we can keep it small enough by doing regenesis regularly, we can fit in RAM 🙂 only transaction senders will need to have full state on disk ok that's true 😆 Though if you phrase it as "we're doing partial-stateless but setting the time-to-live parameter to 1 million blocks" then you get the same benefits and at the same time an upgrade path to even smaller state when ready I actually think that formulating it as "ReGenesis" would be more understandable for most people who are not in the weeds of Stateless Ethereum research hmm I can see how that's better branding, though the brand would make less sense if you do it once every 6 months... I think it will be perfect. Once people understand that we can keep doing it, the light bulb will go on 🙂 we can even do it on a pre-programmed schedule, i.e. without explicit hard-forks each time Then we can put various pieces of the blockchain on Bittorrent, Swarm, IPFS, etc. I mean historical blockchain, pre last ReGenesis Speaking of that... I'm wondering what the progress on doing that for history is (not state) As putting history on such networks is relatively much easier than state and there's fewer applications that need old history Well, this ReGenesis proposal was mostly motivated by desire to solve the large blockchain problem, not so much large state problem The progress otherwise is hampered by the absence of some canonical way of slicing the blockchain into pieces that can be archived and hopefully immortalised So if that's the problem, then I think archiving old history is by far the lowest hanging fruit Only a few applications *need* txs/logs more than 4 months old And it's naturally the easiest thing to put into a bittorrent type system, because the data once committeed is relatively unchangeable archiving the old blockchain does not work without replacing the genesis, to be honest what do you mean by replacing the genesis? lets take turbo-geth as an example. Due to its data model, the only way it can currently sync is to start from genesis, download the blockchain and replay. It can do it very efficiently. But if we take the blocks 1-10m out of the network, then suddently turbo-geth has to go to fetch them somewhere else simply to operate. A better architecture would be if any time we remove a block segment from the network, we advance the genesis, so that we do not effectively make the network dependent on whatever the dominant state snapshot sync is - which I think is a wrong step that is why I gave Cosmos Hub as an example in the beginning they remove the blockchain segment, but they advance the genesis Can't it just fast sync the state at that point? I guess you could also just include the state file in the client code no, we can't. Fast sync is incompatible with our data model and I think we must not make it mandatory because it disallows very serious optimisations So if you "make that state the genesis state", that in practice entails including it as part of the client download, right? Or I suppose you could have a bittorrent for it or whatever well, naively yes. That is why I mention in my post that downloading 40Gb would also be bad experience and to solve this problem, I introduce the transaction witnesses into the system so you hard-code only whatever is the state root of the latest regenesis and yes, you can download the state from bittorrent or fast sync, or whatever but it won't be changing every 15 seconds it will be stable for 6 months, for example and if every client can cope with replaying 6 months of blocks, then we don't need super-duper sync algorithms for most of our activities thank you for this discussion, BTW, really helpful > well, naively yes. That is why I mention in my post that downloading 40Gb would also be bad experience Right, but I feel like going from 200 GB to 40 GB gives 4/5 the benefit for 1/5 the effort So we should "just do it" And of course at the same time keep thinking about how to cut down the 40 by "just do it", you mean the agreement (without even hard forks) that after every 1m blocks will be producing state snapshot + blockchain files and replicating it all over the internet, and stop serving them as part of the sync? perhaps stop serving them at the block X*1m + some time 🙂 <GuthL> You probably want a proof of proof of work alongside the snapshot Oh yes, what are your ideas on that? > by "just do it", you mean the agreement (without even hard forks) that after every 1m blocks will be producing state snapshot + blockchain files and replicating it all over the internet, and stop serving them as part of the sync? Yeah > Oh yes, what are your ideas on that? Probably do it in the same way as it is done by fast sync by verifying the chain of headers up to the genesis? A million of headers is about 1mb worth of data. I believe we can manage to store them alongside with reGenesis state. <GuthL> Have you look into Flyclient by Bunz and al.? https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/226.pdf AFAIK, it is planned to be implemented in Zcash (https://electriccoin.co/blog/explaining-flyclient/ and https://zips.z.cash/zip-0221) <GuthL> I have started a small implementation to create an hybrid mode where you would beam sync from the tip to the Flyclient proof to be fully fast synced. Very similar to what you described. I am sorry, 1 million headers is about 400Mb but anyway this straightforward solution should fit good FlyClient: I remember trying to look into it before, and my question is (perhaps I just need to look into the paper again) - it does seem to require adding MMR commitments into the headers, right? BTW, PoW verification is already probabilistic in go-ethereum, at least: https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/blob/master/core/headerchain.go#L252

excerpts.content: I just published the idea for "ReGenesis": https://ethresear.ch/t/regenesis-resetting-ethereum-to-reduce-the-burden-of-large-blockchain-and-state/7582

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Hmm, not sure I understand this idea

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Is it basically saying that we agree on a one-time event where all state and history before some time X is no longer considered available, and so accessing anything from there requires a witness?

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: yes. And it does not have to be one-time. We can do it regularly

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: That feels like it already incurs most of the complexity of stateless ethereum

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: yes, but it does not requite repricing for the sake of witnesses

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Actually isn't it basically the same as the "half-stateless ethereum where witnesses don't include anything accessed in the last N blocks" but discrete instead of continuous?

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: it is very similar, yes

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: eh IMO we have to do the repricing anyway because the things that are bad for witness size are also bad for DoS attacks at present

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: The DoS vulnerability would be lower with a smaller state size but only logarithmically so

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: I don't think there will be vulnerability, because attacker will have to pay for the proofs

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: no I mean DoS transactions that access a bunch of contracts that are already in the "fresh state"

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: So same sort of thing that an attacker would do today

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: oh, to expand the fresh state?

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: No, to hit disk over and over again

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: As fresh state would still go on disk same as today, right?

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: well, if we can keep it small enough by doing regenesis regularly, we can fit in RAM 🙂

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: only transaction senders will need to have full state on disk

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: ok that's true 😆

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Though if you phrase it as "we're doing partial-stateless but setting the time-to-live parameter to 1 million blocks" then you get the same benefits and at the same time an upgrade path to even smaller state when ready

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: I actually think that formulating it as "ReGenesis" would be more understandable for most people who are not in the weeds of Stateless Ethereum research

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: hmm I can see how that's better branding, though the brand would make less sense if you do it once every 6 months...

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: I think it will be perfect. Once people understand that we can keep doing it, the light bulb will go on 🙂

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: we can even do it on a pre-programmed schedule, i.e. without explicit hard-forks each time

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: Then we can put various pieces of the blockchain on Bittorrent, Swarm, IPFS, etc.

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: I mean historical blockchain, pre last ReGenesis

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Speaking of that... I'm wondering what the progress on doing that for history is (not state)

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: As putting history on such networks is relatively much easier than state and there's fewer applications that need old history

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: Well, this ReGenesis proposal was mostly motivated by desire to solve the large blockchain problem, not so much large state problem

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: The progress otherwise is hampered by the absence of some canonical way of slicing the blockchain into pieces that can be archived and hopefully immortalised

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: So if that's the problem, then I think archiving old history is by far the lowest hanging fruit

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Only a few applications *need* txs/logs more than 4 months old

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: And it's naturally the easiest thing to put into a bittorrent type system, because the data once committeed is relatively unchangeable

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: archiving the old blockchain does not work without replacing the genesis, to be honest

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: what do you mean by replacing the genesis?

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: lets take turbo-geth as an example. Due to its data model, the only way it can currently sync is to start from genesis, download the blockchain and replay. It can do it very efficiently. But if we take the blocks 1-10m out of the network, then suddently turbo-geth has to go to fetch them somewhere else simply to operate. A better architecture would be if any time we remove a block segment from the network, we advance the genesis, so that we do not effectively make the network dependent on whatever the dominant state snapshot sync is - which I think is a wrong step

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: that is why I gave Cosmos Hub as an example in the beginning

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: they remove the blockchain segment, but they advance the genesis

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Can't it just fast sync the state at that point?

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: I guess you could also just include the state file in the client code

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: no, we can't. Fast sync is incompatible with our data model

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: and I think we must not make it mandatory

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: because it disallows very serious optimisations

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: So if you "make that state the genesis state", that in practice entails including it as part of the client download, right?

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Or I suppose you could have a bittorrent for it or whatever

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: well, naively yes. That is why I mention in my post that downloading 40Gb would also be bad experience

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: and to solve this problem, I introduce the transaction witnesses into the system

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: so you hard-code only whatever is the state root of the latest regenesis

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: and yes, you can download the state from bittorrent or fast sync, or whatever

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: but it won't be changing every 15 seconds

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: it will be stable for 6 months, for example

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: and if every client can cope with replaying 6 months of blocks, then we don't need super-duper sync algorithms for most of our activities

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: thank you for this discussion, BTW, really helpful

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: > well, naively yes. That is why I mention in my post that downloading 40Gb would also be bad experience

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Right, but I feel like going from 200 GB to 40 GB gives 4/5 the benefit for 1/5 the effort

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: So we should "just do it"

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: And of course at the same time keep thinking about how to cut down the 40

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: by "just do it", you mean the agreement (without even hard forks) that after every 1m blocks will be producing state snapshot + blockchain files and replicating it all over the internet, and stop serving them as part of the sync?

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: perhaps stop serving them at the block X*1m + some time 🙂

excerpts.content: <GuthL> You probably want a proof of proof of work alongside the snapshot

> by "just do it", you mean the agreement (without even hard forks) that after every 1m blocks will be producing state snapshot + blockchain files and replicating it all over the internet, and stop serving them as part of the sync?

Yeah

> Oh yes, what are your ideas on that?
Probably do it in the same way as it is done by fast sync by verifying the chain of headers up to the genesis? A million of headers is about 1mb worth of data. I believe we can manage to store them alongside with reGenesis state.
